A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Words in Motion research. All 12 pages of v1 and 13 pages of v2, including appendices, figures and mathematical expressions, support reliable comparison across the reorganized material.

before.justification: v1 reports original linear-probing accuracies, embedding-quality measurements, feature-distribution analysis and qualitative motion-control experiments in Sections 5–6 and the appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original probing and motion-control experiments, including additional model results, clustering measurements, control calibration and feature-correlation analyses.

M1.justification: The quantization rules, detached linear probes, PCA construction from opposing hidden states and temperature-scaled activation addition remain. v2 Section 4.3 adds pedestrian-to-vehicle agent control vectors alongside speed, acceleration and direction controls, extending the controllable features without replacing the algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use Argoverse 2 Forecasting and Waymo Open Motion for motion forecasting, feature probing and forecast control. The three qualitative control scenarios are retained. Added architectures and diagnostic analyses do not introduce another dataset, population or input-environment scenario.

E2.justification: Both versions retain uncontrolled forecasts as references and do not evaluate competing interpretability or steering algorithms. HPTR is newly examined using the proposed probing procedure in v2 Figures 2–3; it expands the host-model study rather than the set of alternatives evaluated against that procedure.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes Wayformer from hierarchical fusion with attention-based motion states to early fusion with probes on a three-layer MLP, and adds hierarchical HPTR. AV2 evaluation replaces joint-motion top-1/top-5 reporting with separate acceleration, speed, direction and agent probes. New analyses introduce CDNV, feature correlations and speed-control calibration over temperatures from -50 to 50 using Pearson correlation, R-squared and straightness index.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative examinations of clustering, feature relationships and control linearity through CDNV, Appendix A.6 heatmaps and Figure 5 calibration. It removes v1 Figure 6's comparison between joint-motion probing and the product of component accuracies. The three qualitative control case studies are retained, despite relocation and renumbering.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty across runs. Embedding dispersion and the added correlation and linearity scores serve as diagnostic metrics, rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds and revises AV2 model curves while removing joint-motion results. New RedMotion CDNV values are 0.9499 for Waymo and 2.4598 for AV2; Figure 5 reports Pearson 0.948, R-squared 0.821 and straightness index 0.957. These are additional results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains. Appendix A.3 also corrects the stationary-vehicle attribution to AV2 approximately 51% and Waymo 28%, matching the unchanged distribution data that v1's prose had reversed.

T1.justification: The quantization rules, PCA construction and neural-collapse account are retained. v2 introduces empirical metrics and conceptual discussion of representation hypotheses, but no new formal mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 replaces the abstract's explicit textual-input interface claim with interpretable-feature control and makes meaningful latent directions and distances an explicit contribution. The central claims that motion-model states encode interpretable features and permit inference-time steering remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking embedding dispersion to attention versus MLP encoders, higher AV2 CDNV to longer motion histories, and calibration linearity to controllability. It removes v1's explicit agent-centric scope restriction and acknowledgment that downstream motion planning was not evaluated. HPTR expands the studied representations, but the later discussion of planning applications still lacks downstream evaluation.

D1.justification: v2 newly states hidden dimension 128, supplies HPTR settings and fusion definitions, and describes forecasting metrics in Appendix A.5. Its loss description additionally lists confidence cross-entropy; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an implementation change or fuller documentation. Existing thresholds, optimizer, learning rate, input lengths and code-access information remain, while v1's dataset-size, geographic and future-horizon descriptions are removed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially expands its connections to latent-space regularities, linear representations, superposition and activation steering, including newly cited work by Mikolov, Pennington, Arora, Elhage and Rimsky. Language-interface coverage also broadens beyond driving. Much existing driving literature moves to Appendix A.2, while several forecasting citations associated with v1's introduction and limitations disappear.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work gains structured subsections, methods and settings are reorganized, and forecast control becomes a Results subsection. Thresholds, distributions, training details and much driving-related discussion move into a structured appendix; the standalone Limitations section is removed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around a repeated generic module, AV2 probing panels are reorganized, and a calibration plot with a numerical table plus two heatmaps are added. The distribution chart is reordered, recolored and moved to the appendix. Existing qualitative figures are retained but rearranged and recaptioned, substantially changing the presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the largely probing-based and qualitative evidence in v1 with quantitative clustering and control-calibration results, while examining additional representations and clarifying the feature-control framing. These provide a limited net improvement. Sparse calibration-protocol details and removal of explicit downstream-evaluation limitations temper the gains; the new evidence does not establish broad practical controllability.
